vitriolic

/vit-ree-OL-ik/ - the stress falls on OL · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Vitriolic means filled with bitter, cruel harshness.

The two Victorian orchid hunters filled a decade with vitriolic letters, each accusing the other of theft, fraud, and 'a greenhouse run on lies.'

Example

The town-hall meeting about parking turned vitriolic within minutes — a retired teacher was called a saboteur over a crosswalk, and two neighbors of forty years left by different doors.

Vitriolic is more precise than 'angry' or 'harsh' because it names language with acid in it — bitter, cruel, and meant to burn what it lands on. An angry letter wants to win the argument; a vitriolic one wants to leave a scar.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

poisonous: Poisonous words are meant to injure, like venom worked into words — the harm is the whole intention. Vitriolic overlaps closely but names the chemistry: bitterness like acid, cruel and burning on contact. Poison suggests quiet, hidden damage; vitriol scars in the open, the moment it lands.

savage: A savage attack comes at full, unrestrained force — nothing held back, no line uncrossed. Vitriolic adds bitterness to the force: acid, spite, cruelty savored. A savage review may simply be merciless about the work; a vitriolic one wants the author to feel the burn.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

warmhearted: means well and speaks with warmth

admiring: looks for what deserves praise and says so

Where it sits · how much venom the words carry — sharp → cutting → vitriolic

sharp vs. vitriolic: A sharp remark has an edge but no venom — the mild end of the ladder, far below vitriolic.

cutting vs. vitriolic: Cutting words wound and are meant to, yet they stop short of vitriolic, where the wound is doused in acid — bitterness added for the pleasure of the burn.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vitriol

Root — vitriol: oil of vitriol — the old name for sulfuric acid (from Latin vitrum, 'glass')

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of

Put it together

Put it together: Vitriol (the alchemists' name for sulfuric acid — glassy crystals, from Latin vitrum, 'glass') + -ic (characteristic of) = having the character of acid. The metaphor did what acid does and never let go: vitriolic language is speech that burns through whatever it touches, and the burn is the point.

Word Choice

condemning / vivid

Vitriolic is for language past saving — feuds, flame wars, poison-pen letters. Its unit-mate acerbic is the crucial calibration: acerbic stings with wit and can even improve its target, while vitriolic has burned the wit off and means only to hurt. If you can laugh, it was acerbic; if you flinch, it was vitriolic.
